source: We found that a majority of species had accessory gene pools which were markedly more diverged than core genes, and the few exceptions (e.g., N. gonorrhoeae and N. meningitidis) had small effect sizes.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis across multiple species.

claim: For certain species, gene frequency could act as a recombination barrier.
source: One testable hypothesis consistent with our observation that core genes generally undergo more homologous recombination when compared with accessory genes is that the least frequent genes experience less recombination because they have fewer recombination partners. In other words, gene frequency could act as a recombination barrier.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observations.

claim: Certain species displayed trends consistent with a gene frequency barrier, particularly for the recombination coverage.
source: We found that certain species displayed trends consistent with a gene frequency barrier, particularly for the recombination coverage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: C. jejuni, S. agalactiae, and P. aeruginosa showed trends most consistent with the gene frequency barrier hypothesis when considering recombination rates.
source: When considering the recombination rates (displayed as empirical cumulative distribution functions here because of disparate rates across and within species), C. jejuni, S. agalactiae, and P. aeruginosa showed trends most consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: For some species where cloud genes showed high recombination rates (e.g., N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, E. coli, and S. flexneri), this could be related to the high gene replacement rate experienced by rare genes such as 'ORFans', or diversifying selection experienced by these genes.
source: For some of the exceptions in which cloud genes showed high recombination rates (e.g., N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, E. coli, and S. flexneri), this could be related to the high gene replacement rate experienced by rare genes such as 'ORFans' (Wolf et al., 2016), or diversifying selection experienced by these genes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed exceptions, supported by citation to Wolf et al., 2016.

claim: There is a modest positive correlation between recombination coverage and gene frequency when considering the 50th percentile of the matched parameter distributions for all species.
source: Overall, we see a modest positive correlation with both recombination coverage and rates when considering the 50th and 25th percentiles of the matched parameter distributions for all species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: There is a modest positive correlation between recombination rates and gene frequency when considering the 25th percentile of the matched parameter distributions for all species.
source: Overall, we see a modest positive correlation with both recombination coverage and rates when considering the 50th and 25th percentiles of the matched parameter distributions for all species (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Despite the high gene replacement rates and sequence variability experienced by some accessory genes, core genes experience markedly higher recombination rates than the accessory genes in S. pneumoniae.
source: We found that despite the high gene replacement rates and sequence variability experienced by some accessory genes (Iranzo et al., 2019; Kuenne et al., 2013; Kuhn et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2016), core genes experience markedly higher recombination rates than the accessory genes in S. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by citations to Iranzo et al., 2019; Kuenne et al., 2013; Kuhn et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2016.

claim: In 8 out of 12 microbial species, higher recombination rates are observed in core genes relative to accessory genes.
source: In 8 out of 12 microbial species, we observe higher recombination rates in core genes relative to accessory genes.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the data analysis.

claim: In a subset of microbial species, the magnitude of the effect of higher recombination rates in core genes is large (e.g., S. pneumoniae, E. coli, S. flexneri, N. meningitidis, and C. jejuni).
source: In a subset of microbial species, the magnitude of the effect is large (e.g., S. pneumoniae, E. coli, S. flexneri, N. meningitidis, and C. jejuni).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the data analysis.

claim: Some work has previously shown housekeeping and core genes can experience extensive recombination consistent with the results of this study.
source: While some work has previously shown housekeeping (Vos and Didelot, 2009) and core genes (Lin and Kussell, 2017; Park and Andam, 2020) can experience extensive recombination consistent with our results, our work offers a direct, quantitative comparison between the core and accessory genomes spanning multiple species and >100,000 sampled genomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vos and Didelot, 2009; Lin and Kussell, 2017; Park and Andam, 2020.

claim: Some members of the Neisseriaceae (e.g., N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae) and Pasteurellaceae families (e.g., H. influenzae) have DNA uptake sequences and uptake signal sequences accumulated in their core genomes which promote homologous recombination.
source: In certain species, mechanisms that give rise to higher recombination rates in the core genome are known; for example, some members of the Neisseriaceae (e.g., N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae) and Pasteurellaceae families (e.g., H. influenzae) have DNA uptake sequences and uptake signal sequences accumulated in their core genomes which promote homologous recombination (Frye et al., 2013; Treangen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frye et al., 2013; Treangen et al., 2008.

claim: In S. pneumoniae, core gene pools had lower mutational divergence relative to accessory gene pools.
source: We found that in S. pneumoniae, core gene pools had lower mutational divergence relative to accessory gene pools.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: For the majority of the species analyzed, core gene pools had lower mutational divergence, and 9 out of 12 species analyzed had large effect sizes indicating core gene pools have lower mutational divergence (Cohen's d = 0.92–2.8).
source: Furthermore, we found that for the majority of the species we analyzed this was the case, and 9 out of 12 species analyzed had large effect sizes indicating core gene pools have lower mutational divergence (Cohen's d = 0.92–2.8).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Previous studies indicate that the core genome is under strong, purifying selection.
source: Previous studies indicate that the core genome is under strong, purifying selection (Bohlin et al., 2014; Bohlin et al., 2017; den Bakker et al., 2013; McInerney et al., 2017; Moulana et al., 2020), and it is well known that purifying selection reduces mean coalescence times (Charlesworth et al., 1993; Nicolaisen and Desai, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bohlin et al., 2014; Bohlin et al., 2017; den Bakker et al., 2013; McInerney et al., 2017; Moulana et al., 2020.

claim: It is well known that purifying selection reduces mean coalescence times.
source: Previous studies indicate that the core genome is under strong, purifying selection (Bohlin et al., 2014; Bohlin et al., 2017; den Bakker et al., 2013; McInerney et al., 2017; Moulana et al., 2020), and it is well known that purifying selection reduces mean coalescence times (Charlesworth et al., 1993; Nicolaisen and Desai, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Charlesworth et al., 1993; Nicolaisen and Desai, 2012.

claim: Some accessory genes are used for niche specialization.
source: An additional consideration is that some accessory genes are used for niche specialization (Azarian et al., 2020; McInerney et al., 2017; Vernikos et al., 2015); if different alleles of the same accessory gene are adaptive to different niches, this could result in allelic diversity due to balancing selection, which would increase coalescence times of accessory genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Azarian et al., 2020; McInerney et al., 2017; Vernikos et al., 2015.

claim: If different alleles of the same accessory gene are adaptive to different niches, this could result in allelic diversity due to balancing selection, which would increase coalescence times of accessory genes.
source: An additional consideration is that some accessory genes are used for niche specialization (Azarian et al., 2020; McInerney et al., 2017; Vernikos et al., 2015); if different alleles of the same accessory gene are adaptive to different niches, this could result in allelic diversity due to balancing selection, which would increase coalescence times of accessory genes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on inference.

claim: Evidence from long-term microbial evolution experiments has shown that on average the synonymous substitution rate is fairly homogeneous across the core and accessory genomes.
source: Accordingly, evidence from long-term microbial evolution experiments has shown that on average the synonymous substitution rate is fairly homogeneous across the core and accessory genomes (Maddamsetti et al., 2015; Maddamsetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maddamsetti et al., 2015; Maddamsetti et al., 2017.

claim: Experiments in numerous species show that homologous recombination rates decay with increasing sequence divergence.
source: Experiments in numerous species show that homologous recombination rates decay with increasing sequence divergence (Fraser et al., 2007; Majewski, 2001; Majewski et al., 2000; Vulić et al., 1997; Zawadzki et al., 1995), and the role of this recombination barrier in bacterial speciation has been analyzed (Falush et al., 2006; Hanage et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fraser et al., 2007; Majewski, 2001; Majewski et al., 2000; Vulić et al., 1997; Zawadzki et al., 1995.

claim: The role of the recombination barrier (decay with increasing sequence divergence) in bacterial speciation has been analyzed.
source: Experiments in numerous species show that homologous recombination rates decay with increasing sequence divergence (Fraser et al., 2007; Majewski, 2001; Majewski et al., 2000; Vulić et al., 1997; Zawadzki et al., 1995), and the role of this recombination barrier in bacterial speciation has been analyzed (Falush et al., 2006; Hanage et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Falush et al., 2006; Hanage et al., 2006b.

claim: The effect of recombination rates decaying with sequence divergence is primarily ascribed to the ubiquity of RecA and mismatch repair systems, both of which are essential for recombination and whose molecular mechanisms depend on sequence similarity.
source: This effect is primarily ascribed to the ubiquity of RecA and mismatch repair systems, both of which are essential for recombination and whose molecular mechanisms depend on sequence similarity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about molecular mechanisms of recombination.

claim: The higher recombination rates and lower pool divergence observed for the core genome of S. pneumoniae and several other microbial species may suggest that the increased homology of the core genes reduces the barrier for homologous recombination in this part of the genome.
source: Consistent with these experimental and analytical results, the higher recombination rates and lower pool divergence we observe here for the core genome of S. pneumoniae and several other microbial species may suggest that the increased homology of the core genes reduces the barrier for homologous recombination in this part of the genome.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claim: Modeling has suggested that homologous recombination slows sequence divergence in the core genome by homogenizing this part of the genome, whereas accessory genes do not have the opportunity to be homogenized as they are subject to continual gene gain and loss.
source: This is also in line with modeling, which has suggested that homologous recombination slows sequence divergence in the core genome by homogenizing this part of the genome, whereas accessory genes do not have the opportunity to be homogenized as they are subject to continual gene gain and loss (Iranzo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iranzo et al., 2019.

claim: An evolutionary feedback loop may operate in certain species of bacteria: purifying selection acting on core genes causes higher levels of homology at these loci, this increases their homologous recombination rates, which in turn enables more efficient purifying selection by breaking linkages between genes.
source: Thus, we propose that an evolutionary feedback loop may operate in certain species of bacteria: purifying selection acting on core genes causes higher levels of homology at these loci, this increases their homologous recombination rates, which in turn enables more efficient purifying selection by breaking linkages between genes, effectively minimizing Hill–Robertson interference and hitchhiking effects (Barton, 1995; Barton, 2010; Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976) across the core genome.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings, supported by citations to Barton, 1995; Barton, 2010; Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976.

claim: The proposed evolutionary feedback loop would effectively minimize Hill–Robertson interference and hitchhiking effects across the core genome.
source: Thus, we propose that an evolutionary feedback loop may operate in certain species of bacteria: purifying selection acting on core genes causes higher levels of homology at these loci, this increases their homologous recombination rates, which in turn enables more efficient purifying selection by breaking linkages between genes, effectively minimizing Hill–Robertson interference and hitchhiking effects (Barton, 1995; Barton, 2010; Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976) across the core genome.
evidence: This is part of the speculative proposal, supported by citations to Barton, 1995; Barton, 2010; Felsenstein and Yokoyama, 1976.

claim: The work suggests that another recombination barrier for accessory genes may be related to their lower abundance in the population.
source: Moreover, our work suggests that another recombination barrier for accessory genes may be related to their lower abundance in the population, as we found that the levels of homologous recombination are correlated with gene frequency in a subset of species.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The levels of homologous recombination are correlated with gene frequency in a subset of species.
source: Moreover, our work suggests that another recombination barrier for accessory genes may be related to their lower abundance in the population, as we found that the levels of homologous recombination are correlated with gene frequency in a subset of species.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The work contributes broadly to understanding of how selection and recombination act to shape diversity.
source: In summary, we have presented a quantitative analysis of the variation in recombination rates between core and accessory genomes. As these two parts of the genome are under different forms of selective pressures, this work contributes broadly to our understanding of how selection and recombination act to shape diversity.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the work.

claim: The expansion of this approach to more specific gene classes could lead to a better understanding of how selective pressure and homologous recombination interplay to shape niche-adaptive genes.
source: The expansion of this approach to more specific gene classes could lead to a better understanding of how selective pressure and homologous recombination interplay to shape niche-adaptive genes such as those involved with drug resistance and antigen variation, for which allele shuffling due to homologous recombination can play a central role in their evolution (Bowler et al., 1994; Maiden, 1998; Seifert, 1996).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications, supported by citations to Bowler et al., 1994; Maiden, 1998; Seifert, 1996.

claim: For niche-adaptive genes such as those involved with drug resistance and antigen variation, allele shuffling due to homologous recombination can play a central role in their evolution.
source: The expansion of this approach to more specific gene classes could lead to a better understanding of how selective pressure and homologous recombination interplay to shape niche-adaptive genes such as those involved with drug resistance and antigen variation, for which allele shuffling due to homologous recombination can play a central role in their evolution (Bowler et al., 1994; Maiden, 1998; Seifert, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bowler et al., 1994; Maiden, 1998; Seifert, 1996.
